# Summary of Information on Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a Polish pioneering computer engineer born into a family of intellectuals and alpinists. Despite severe injuries during World War II, including temporary blindness and paralysis from a gunshot, he actively participated in the Polish resistance and the Warsaw Uprising, earning three Crosses of Valour. Post-war, he graduated from Warsaw University of Technology in 1951 and embarked on innovative projects in computing and automation.
Karpiński's early work included the vacuum tube-based Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics (AAH) in 1957 and the creation of AKAT-1 (1959), the world's first transistor-based differential equations analyzer. He later developed the Polish perceptron (1964), one of the earliest neural network devices, and the KAR-65 computer (1968), notable for its asynchronicity and speed. His flagship project, the K-202 minicomputer, built with Intel 4004 chips, was revolutionary—featuring modularity, floating point representation, and advanced memory segmentation—but failed to reach mass production due to political obstruction and competing state projects in communist Poland. After political struggles and declining support, Karpiński left the computer industry in 1978 to pursue other work in Switzerland and later returned to Poland.
Karpiński's cooperation with Polish intelligence during his UNESCO-sponsored scholarship visit to the US in the 1960s sparked controversy; while he considered his cooperation limited to technological reporting, later monitoring and surveillance intensified, eventually treating him as a target. His technical achievements remain debated, with some historians comparing him to technological visionaries, while others point to practical limitations. Karpiński was posthumously honored with the Commander's Cross of Polonia Restituta in 2010.
